title: Interest
summary: Interest may be taxed in the recipient's residence State and also in the source State, capped at 10 per cent where the beneficial owner lives in the other State. The Commentary explains the compromise behind source taxation, optional exemptions (government, export finance, banks, credit sales, pension funds), beneficial ownership, the definition of 'interest', the source rule and excessive interest between related parties.
readingNote: Saudi treaties set their own interest rates (often 5 per cent or less) and many exempt interest paid to the other State, its central bank or government agencies. ZATCA's January 2025 circular also says late-payment penalties are not interest.

entries.t: Interest is remuneration on money lent, a type of income from movable capital. Unlike dividends, it does not suffer economic double taxation, because it is generally deductible for the payer.
Like dividends, interest is usually taxed by deduction at source when paid, mainly for practical reasons: the tax withheld can work as an advance on the recipient's own tax.
Exclusive taxation by either State would not win general approval, so a compromise was adopted: residence taxation, plus limited source taxation.
Whether a payer can deduct interest paid to non-residents is a non-discrimination question under Article 24(4).
Interest arising in one State and paid to a resident of the other may be taxed in the residence State, which does not get an exclusive right.
Only interest arising in a Contracting State is covered. Third-State interest and interest attributable to a PE in the other State fall under Article 21.

sections.heading: Paragraph 2: the 10 per cent cap and optional exemptions

entries.t: The source State may tax, but no more than 10 per cent of the gross amount. This is a reasonable maximum given that the residence State also taxes and the source State can already tax business profits through PEs.
Gross source taxation can obstruct trade or be inappropriate, for example where the lender has borrowed to fund the loan, because the tax can exceed its actual profit margin.
States may add a paragraph giving the residence State the sole right to tax certain categories of interest, examples of which follow.
Interest paid to the other State, its political subdivisions, local authorities or central bank is often exempted, at least for governmental activities.
Where the payer is the State itself, source tax may in practice be borne by that State through higher rates, so exempting interest paid by governments can make sense.
Interest on loans made, guaranteed or insured under public export-financing programmes is often exempted bilaterally.

Interest paid to banks and other financial institutions is a strong candidate for exemption, because gross taxation ignores their cost of funds. States need to consider safeguards against abuse, such as back-to-back loans.

Interest on credit sales of equipment, goods or services between enterprises can be exempted. These terms cover sales of whole units and components, and sales financed through a general line of credit from the seller.
Interest paid to exempt pension funds and similar entities may be exempted to keep their domestic and foreign investments neutral.
Instead of exemption, States may agree a lower rate for any category, or add other categories.

BEPS addressed low-taxed recipients that do not distribute their profits. Article 29 deals with the treaty-shopping side, and States may also use the Article 1 Commentary provisions on preferential regimes.
Beneficial ownership clarifies 'paid to a resident'. It is read in context, not in a technical domestic-law sense.
Agents, nominees and conduit companies with very narrow powers over the income are not beneficial owners, so the source State need not grant relief.

The test is whether the recipient's right to use and enjoy the interest is constrained by a contractual or legal obligation to pass the payment on. This may be shown by documents or facts, and must relate to the payment received.
Beneficial ownership does not guarantee the cap. Article 29 and the anti-abuse principles still apply.
The treaty meaning differs from 'beneficial owner' in anti-money-laundering rules.
The cap still applies where an agent or nominee is interposed for a beneficial owner resident in the other State.
The method and procedure for source taxation are left to domestic law, as is whether relief depends on residence taxation. Residence-State relief is dealt with in Articles 23 A and 23 B.

Interest means income from debt-claims of every kind, secured or not and with or without profit participation, including cash deposits, government securities, bonds and debentures. Mortgage interest is included even where some States treat it as income from immovable property. Profit-participating debt-claims remain loans if the contract clearly shows a loan at interest.
Interest on participating bonds, and on convertible bonds before conversion, is normally interest. It is treated as a dividend only if the loan effectively shares the debtor's business risks.

For securities, premiums and prizes count as interest: broadly, whatever the issuer pays above the amount the subscriber paid, such as issue discounts and redemption premiums. A capital gain or loss on selling the security is not interest.

When a bond is sold, the price usually includes accrued interest. Source States generally tax only the buyer on the full interest later paid. Some tax the seller on accrued interest, for example on a sale to an exempt entity, which the definition allows. They should then not tax the same amount again in the buyer's hands.
The definition is in principle exhaustive, with no fallback to domestic law, because it already covers almost all forms of interest and gives legal certainty.
Payments under non-traditional instruments with no underlying debt, such as interest rate swaps, are not interest, unless a loan is in substance present.

Penalty charges for late payment, whether under the contract, customary or set by a court, are excluded: they compensate the creditor for the delay rather than being income from capital. States may omit this exclusion, and may also exclude from Article 11 any interest they intend to treat as dividends.

Annuities are not interest. Annuities for past employment fall under Article 18, and splitting purchased annuities into interest and capital would be difficult for many States, which often tax them like salaries and pensions.

sections.heading: Paragraph 4: interest connected with a PE

entries.t: Interest on a debt-claim effectively connected with a PE in the source State is taxed there under Article 7, without the cap. This is not a force of attraction.
Moving loans into a PE purely to get preferential treatment is usually stopped by Article 29 and the anti-abuse principles. Recording a loan in a PE's books is not enough.
A debt-claim is effectively connected if its economic ownership is allocated to the PE under the OECD report on attributing profits to PEs. Insurance PEs follow Part IV of the report.

Interest arises in the payer's State of residence. The exception is interest on a loan with an obvious economic link to a PE that the payer has in the other State and that bears the interest: it arises where the PE is.

Without that economic link, the PE State cannot tax the interest, not even through a 'taxable quota'. The link is clear where the PE itself borrowed for its own needs and pays the interest, or where head office borrowed solely for that PE, which bears the interest. A loan used for several PEs in different countries falls outside the rule, since one loan cannot have several sources. States may narrow or widen this bilaterally.

Triangular case: payer and recipient are residents of the two Contracting States, but the loan finances the payer's PE in a third State. The Convention does not resolve this, so double taxation can arise. States can agree alternative wording that treats such interest as arising in the PE State.
If States give the residence State the exclusive right to tax interest, the source rule becomes unnecessary, although it may still matter for Article 23.

sections.heading: Paragraph 6: excessive interest between related parties

entries.t: Where a special relationship makes the interest exceed an arm's length amount, the Article applies only to the arm's length part, and the excess is taxed under each State's law, subject to the rest of the Convention.
The special relationship covers control and common control, family ties, and any community of interests apart from the loan itself.

The excess is classified by its actual nature. As drafted, the paragraph adjusts only the rate, not a recharacterisation of the loan as equity. With the suggested wording changes it can also cover loan amounts or terms that would not have been agreed at arm's length. The source State may also disallow the excess deduction if its law allows.
If the two States would tax the excess under different Articles, they should resolve this through the mutual agreement procedure.

membersNote: Paragraph 37 is an observation (Canada and the United Kingdom), and paragraphs 38 to 46 are reservations on the Article. Non-OECD economies' positions are in section P(11).
